data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference of future success, but as a non-inductive methodological rule grounded in 'verisimilitude' (truth-likeness) and the logic of severe testing: choosing the theory that has withstood the most stringent attempts at falsification maximizes our proximity to truth without assigning it higher probability. This preference survives the charge of smuggling in induction only if we accept the cost of abandoning any guarantee that the future will resemble the past, treating the choice as a rational gamble based on current explanatory power rather than a prediction of reliability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If verisimilitude cannot be formally defined or measured without relying on inductive assumptions about the structure of the world, the defense collapses into cryptic induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the pragmatic necessity of acting (e.g., building a bridge) logically entails an assumption that nature is uniform, then Popper's separation of action from induction is illusory.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'severe testing' itself presupposes that past falsifications are relevant to future performance, the criterion of severity is circular.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'corroboration' (a report of past performance under severe tests) and 'probability' (a logical relation predicting future frequency). It argues that preferring the better-corroborated theory is a procedural commitment to the theory with the highest content that has not yet been falsified, which Popper equates with having the highest potential verisimilitude. The preference is justified by the goal of science (finding true theories) and the fact that a severely tested theory offers more opportunities for error detection than an untested one; thus, acting on it is the most rational way to pursue truth, even if it offers no inductive assurance of practical success.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
